                          Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of Brian C. Andrews


1                                         I. INTRODUCTION

2   Q         PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

3   A         Brian C. Andrews. My business address is 16690 Swingley Ridge Road, Suite 140,

4             Chesterfield, MO 63017.



5   Q         ARE YOU THE SAME BRIAN C. ANDREWS WHO FILED DIRECT TESTIMONY IN THIS

6             PROCEEDING?

7   A         Yes. I filed Direct Testimony and Exhibits BCA-1 through BCA-3 on behalf of Glenn Hodge

8             and Ryan Hodge, JT Carothers Holdings LLC, MCP 18 LLC, and Schwertner Farms, Inc.

9             on May 13th, 2026.




        SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
        PUC Docket No. 59475
        Page 4                          BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1   Q         WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

 2   A         The purpose of my Cross-Rebuttal Testimony is to respond to certain assertions made by

 3             other parties’ witnesses in their Direct Testimonies filed in this proceeding. Specifically, I

 4             respond to the Direct Testimonies of Dr. Joshua Rhodes (on behalf of Solana Ranch /

 5             Ringler), Dr. Mark Turnbough (on behalf of Wulff Bluff Creek Ranch / Abell Ranches),

 6             Ms. Karen Smith Hubbard (on behalf of Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed), and Mr. Jason A.

 7             Howton (pro se), and Mr. James E. Scott, III (on behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company).

 8             Each of these witnesses opposes Route 894 and recommends alternative routes or, in

 9             Mr. Scott’s case, a fundamentally different analytical framework.

10                    My silence regarding any other testimony or issue should not be taken as an

11             endorsement of any position taken by any party in this proceeding.



12   Q         CAN YOU PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR CROSS-REBUTTAL CONCLUSIONS?

13   A         My conclusions are as follows:

14             1. I continue to agree with the Joint Applicants that Route 894 is the route that best
15                addresses the requirements of PURA and PUC Substantive Rule Section 25.101 for
16                the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project.

17             2. Dr. Rhodes and Dr. Turnbough both recommend Route 392. Route 392 costs
18                approximately $34 million more than Route 894 and has 136 habitable structures
19                within 500 feet of the route centerline, compared to 85 for Route 894. The habitable
20                structure breakdown shows that 124 of Route 392’s 136 structures are single-family
21                residences. Forty of those single-family residences are concentrated on a single link,
22                Link E12, which is only 3.73 miles long. Route 392 does not provide a combination of
23                routing factor performance that supports selection over Route 894.

24             3. Ms. Hubbard recommends seven alternative routes, with particular emphasis on
25                Routes 891 and 895. Routes 891 and 895 were not filed routes and have no cost
26                data. Both have 108 habitable structures within 500 feet, of which 102 are single-
27                family residences. Her proposal to give less weight to habitable structures already
28                near existing transmission lines is also inconsistent with how the Commission and
29                ALJs have evaluated prudent avoidance in previous transmission line proceedings.

30             4. Mr. Howton opposes Links F20 and F23. Route 899, which I identified in my Direct
31                Testimony as a viable alternative to Route 894, avoids both of those links while
32                maintaining 85 habitable structures and an estimated cost of approximately
33                $1.683 billion. Mr. Howton’s recommended alternatives (Routes 296, 767, 551, 546,


         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 5                            BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1                and 194) all have more habitable structures than Routes 894 and 899, ranging from
 2                95 to 151.

 3             5. Mr. Scott challenges the Applicants’ routing methodology and recommends use of the
 4                EPRI-GTC suitability modeling framework. While methodological improvements to the
 5                routing process may warrant future consideration, this accelerated CCN proceeding is
 6                not the venue for that challenge. The Commission has evaluated and approved
 7                transmission line routes using the routing factors in PURA and Substantive Rule
 8                Section 25.101 for many years. Mr. Scott’s own ranking of the 122 filed routes
 9                identifies ten routes, all in the U6 Corridor, that are uniformly more expensive, longer,
10                and in most cases impact more habitable structures than Route 894. Under the
11                comparative record in this proceeding, Mr. Scott’s analysis does not support selection
12                of a route superior to Route 894.



13                          II. RESPONSE TO DR. JOSHUA RHODES
14                         AND DR. MARK TURNBOUGH (ROUTE 392)

15   Q         WHY DO YOU ADDRESS DR. RHODES AND DR. TURNBOUGH TOGETHER?

16   A         Both witnesses recommend Route 392, and their principal arguments overlap

17             substantially. Dr. Rhodes recommends Route 392 based on his preference for Link U3 at

18             the Colorado River crossing, his argument that pipeline paralleling should be disfavored,

19             and his critique of the Applicants’ habitable structure and property boundary data.

20             Dr. Turnbough also recommends Route 392 based on the Colorado River crossing, his

21             critique of property boundary data, and his characterization of the habitable structure

22             difference between Route 392 and Route 894 as “numerically insignificant.” Addressing

23             these arguments together avoids unnecessary repetition.



24   Q         DR. RHODES AND DR. TURNBOUGH BOTH ARGUE THAT THE COLORADO RIVER

25             CROSSING SHOULD USE LINK U3 RATHER THAN THE LINKS USED BY ROUTE

26             894,    BECAUSE          LINK    U3     PARALLELS         EXISTING        TRANSMISSION

27             INFRASTRUCTURE. WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE?

28   A         The trade-off does not favor Route 392. The switch from Route 894’s Colorado River

29             crossing to Link U3 and Route 392 reduces the length not parallel to existing transmission


         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 6                           BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1             lines by approximately 12 miles. In exchange for that increased paralleling, Route 392

 2             costs approximately $34 million more than Route 894 ($1,715,218,000 versus

 3             $1,680,919,000) and has 136 habitable structures within 500 feet, compared to 85 for

 4             Route 894. That is 51 additional habitable structures, a 60% increase.

 5                    The Commission considers all routing factors and no factor is dispositive, but it has

 6             historically emphasized cost and habitable structures as the two most important routing

 7             factors except when unique circumstances prevail. In its Final Order in Docket No. 30168,

 8             the Commission noted it has emphasized two factors in deciding the routing of

 9             transmission lines: (1) the cost of the line and (2) its impact on habitable structures.

10             Gaining approximately 12 miles of paralleling existing transmission lines at a cost of

11             $34 million and 51 additional habitable structures is a trade-off that does not favor

12             Route 392 under the Commission’s framework.



13   Q         DR. RHODES ARGUES THAT ROUTES WITH PIPELINE PARALLELING SHOULD BE

14             DISFAVORED. WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE?

15   A         Route 894 has 2.29 miles parallel to pipeline on a 223-mile route, which is approximately

16             1% of the total route length. This is a negligible amount of pipeline paralleling. Dr. Rhodes

17             builds his pipeline avoidance criterion into a screening filter that eliminates routes from

18             consideration, but the amount of pipeline paralleling on Route 894 is so small that the

19             criterion has no practical relevance to the route he is attempting to eliminate.

20                    I would also note that the Commission’s removal of pipelines from the list of

21             compatible ROW in 2015 (PUC Project No. 42740) means that pipeline paralleling no




         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 7                            BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1             longer receives credit as a positive factor. It does not mean that proximity to a pipeline is

 2             a negative factor. 1



 3   Q         DR. RHODES IDENTIFIES SEVERAL HABITABLE STRUCTURES THAT HE

 4             BELIEVES ARE MISCHARACTERIZED OR MISSING FROM THE APPLICANTS’

 5             DATA. WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE?

 6   A         The Applicants’ habitable structure data was developed using a consistent methodology

 7             applied uniformly across the entire study area for all 122 filed routes. Dr. Rhodes identifies

 8             a handful of structures along selected segments that he believes are false positives or

9              missed buildings, but he did not conduct a comprehensive review of every structure across

10             every route.    Unless such a comprehensive review has been conducted, identifying

11             isolated potential errors along selected segments does not establish that the data

12             systematically favors any particular route over another. Whatever margin of error exists

13             in the data likely would apply in all directions across all routes.

14                     I would also note that Dr. Rhodes acknowledges the Applicants’ data is

15             “directionally informative” and relies on it for his own route comparison. If the data is

16             reliable enough to support his comparison, it is reliable enough to support the Applicants’

17             comparison and my own.




              1 Rulemaking to Amend Substantive Rule 25.101 Relating to Certification Criteria, Project No.

     42740 (Apr. 22, 2015). (“This intentional omission of pipelines from the list of compatible rights-of-way
     is intended to remove any preference for paralleling or utilizing pipeline rights-of-way while not
     prohibiting such consideration.”)


         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 8                             BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1   Q         DR. RHODES AND DR. TURNBOUGH BOTH CRITICIZE THE APPLICANTS’

 2             PROPERTY BOUNDARY PARALLELING DATA. DR. TURNBOUGH SPECIFICALLY

 3             IDENTIFIES INSTANCES WHERE “APPARENT PROPERTY BOUNDARIES” CROSS

 4             LAND WITH THE SAME OWNER ON BOTH SIDES. WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE?

 5   A         The same analytical framework applies. Utilities in these proceedings collect property

 6             boundary paralleling data using a consistent methodology applied uniformly across the

 7             entire study area. Dr. Turnbough identifies specific instances on Links K51 and K13 where

 8             he believes the property boundary data overstates paralleling, but he did not review every

 9             parcel boundary on every link across all 122 routes. Without a comprehensive review,

10             these isolated observations do not establish systematic bias favoring Route 894 over

11             Route 392 or any other alternative.

12                    Further, property boundary paralleling is only one component of overall compatible

13             ROW paralleling, which also includes paralleling of existing transmission lines, public

14             roads and highways, and railroads. Dr. Turnbough’s own comparison shows the total

15             compatible ROW paralleling percentages for Route 894 and Route 392 are nearly identical

16             (approximately 45.53% and 45.52%, respectively). At effective parity on total paralleling,

17             the remaining distinction between the routes falls to other factors, including cost and

18             habitable structures, where Route 894 has a substantial advantage.



19   Q         DR.   TURNBOUGH          CHARACTERIZES            THE     DIFFERENCE     IN     HABITABLE

20             STRUCTURES        BETWEEN       ROUTE       894    (85)   AND   ROUTE     392    (136)   AS

21             “NUMERICALLY INSIGNIFICANT.” DO YOU AGREE?

22   A         No. Route 392 has 51 more habitable structures within 500 feet of the route centerline

23             than Route 894. That is a 60% increase. To better understand the significance of this

24             difference, I reviewed the habitable structure breakdown by type for Route 392. Of Route

25             392’s 136 habitable structures, 124 are single-family residences, 7 are mobile living units,


         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 9                            BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1             2 are barns, garages, or sheds, and 3 are commercial or industrial buildings. The 51

 2             additional structures on Route 392 compared to Route 894 include 44 additional

 3             single-family residences. Those are 44 additional residences on Route 392 located within

 4             500 feet of a 765-kV transmission line.

 5                       Route 392 uses Link E12, which is significant to several of the landowners

 6             sponsoring my testimony. Link E12 is 3.73 miles long and has 40 habitable structures

 7             within 500 feet. Every one of those 40 structures is a single-family residence. That is

 8             approximately 10.7 single-family residences per mile on a single link. Nearly a third of

 9             Route 392’s total habitable structure count is concentrated in less than 2% of its route

10             length.

11                       Characterizing 51 additional habitable structures as “numerically insignificant” is

12             inconsistent with how the Commission has historically applied the habitable structure

13             factor. The Commission in Docket No. 30168 identified habitable structures as one of the

14             two factors it has emphasized most in deciding the routing of transmission lines.



15   Q         DR. TURNBOUGH ARGUES THAT THE COST DIFFERENCE BETWEEN ROUTE 894

16             AND ROUTE 392 IS “FALSE PRECISION.” WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE?

17   A         If cost differences at this magnitude are too unreliable to credit in favor of Route 894, then

18             they are equally unreliable for any route in this proceeding.        The practical effect of

19             Dr. Turnbough’s argument is to remove cost as a distinguishing factor entirely. If cost is

20             set aside, the remaining primary distinction between Route 894 and Route 392 falls to

21             habitable structures, where Route 894 has 85 and Route 392 has 136.               The “false

22             precision” argument, if accepted, strengthens the case for Route 894.




         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 10                             BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1                        III. RESPONSE TO KAREN SMITH HUBBARD

 2   Q         MS. HUBBARD RECOMMENDS SEVEN ALTERNATIVE ROUTES AND ARGUES

 3             THAT THEY OUTPERFORM ROUTE 894 ON COST, LENGTH, PARALLELING, AND

 4             ENVIRONMENTAL INTEGRITY. WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE?

 5   A         The following table summarizes the habitable structure counts and estimated costs for

 6             Ms. Hubbard’s recommended routes compared to Route 894:


                                                             Table 1

                                              Comparison of Route 894 to
                                         Ms. Hubbard's Recommended Routes

                                                           Habitable
                                        Route              Structures        Estimated Cost

                                         894                    85           $1,680,919,000

                                         524                   140           $1,664,126,000
                                         535                   173           $1,666,210,000
                                         652                   146            Not provided
                                         891                   108            Not provided
                                         895                   108            Not provided
                                         900                   139           $1,661,594,000
                                         905                   172           $1,663,682,000


 7                    Every one of Ms. Hubbard’s seven routes has more habitable structures within

 8             500 feet of the route centerline than Route 894. Her two preferred routes, Routes 891

9              and 895, have 108 habitable structures each, which is 27% more than Route 894’s 85.

10             Routes 535 and 905 have 172 and 173 habitable structures, respectively, more than

11             double Route 894’s count.

12                    The cost differences Ms. Hubbard identifies are modest. For the four routes with

13             available cost data, the savings range from approximately $15 to $20 million on a project



         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 11                               BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1             with a total estimated cost exceeding $1.6 billion, a difference of roughly 1%. This is within

 2             the range the Commission has historically treated as comparable, particularly when

 3             weighed against the habitable structure differential.



 4   Q         MS. HUBBARD RECOMMENDS ROUTES 891 AND 895 WITH PARTICULAR

 5             EMPHASIS. WHAT DO YOU OBSERVE ABOUT THOSE ROUTES?

 6   A         Routes 891 and 895 were not among the 122 routes filed with the Application, and

 7             Ms. Hubbard acknowledges that cost data was not provided for either route. The absence

 8             of cost data for Ms. Hubbard’s two preferred routes is a significant gap in the available

9              data, as cost is one of the factors the Commission has historically weighted most heavily.

10                    Even setting aside the absence of cost data, Routes 891 and 895 each have 108

11             habitable structures, 23 more than Route 894. To evaluate Ms. Hubbard’s argument that

12             “not all habitable structures are the same,” I reviewed the habitable structure breakdown

13             by type for Routes 891, 895, and 894:


                                                         Table 2

                                         Habital Structures By Route and Type

                                                  Mobile         Barn,
                             Single Family        Living        Garage,
                  Route       Residence            Unit         or Shed      Commercial         Total
                    894             80               3               2             0              85
                    891            102               4               2             0             108
                    895            102               4               2             0             108


14                    The composition is essentially identical across all three routes: approximately 94%

15             single-family residences. The 23 additional structures on Routes 891 and 895 compared

16             to Route 894 include 22 additional single-family residences. Ms. Hubbard argues that a



         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 12                           BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1             “junkyard would not have the same concerns and characteristics as a home for older

 2             individuals,” but the data shows the additional structures on her preferred routes are

 3             overwhelmingly the same type she identifies as deserving the most consideration:

 4             single-family homes where families live.



 5   Q         MS. HUBBARD ARGUES THAT HABITABLE STRUCTURES ALREADY IN CLOSE

 6             PROXIMITY TO EXISTING TRANSMISSION LINES SHOULD NOT RECEIVE THE

 7             SAME CONSIDERATION. HAS THIS ARGUMENT BEEN BROUGHT UP BEFORE?

 8   A         Yes. In 2011, SOAH ALJs rejected this argument. In Docket No. 38597, Application of

 9             Oncor Electric Delivery LLC to Amend a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for the

10             Krum West to Anna 345-kV CREZ Transmission Line, certain parties argued that the

11             impact on habitable structures near a particular link should be given less weight because

12             a transmission line already existed along that link, and those structures would not be

13             “newly impacted in the same way.” In the Proposal for Decision, the ALJs found “no merit”

14             to that argument, explaining that there is no legal distinction between affecting habitable

15             structures that are already in proximity to an existing line and those that are not. The ALJs

16             reasoned that either scenario increases potential exposures to electric and magnetic

17             fields, and that prudent avoidance dictates that both scenarios should be limited when

18             reasonably practical. The ALJs focused on the number of habitable structures along a

19             line, rather than making a distinction about which habitable structures are already near

20             existing lines.

21                     The Commission reinforced this position in Docket No. 45622, Application of

22             Sharyland Utilities, L.P. to Amend Its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for the

23             CREZ Second Circuit Upgrade Project. In that proceeding, which involved adding a

24             second circuit to existing single-circuit CREZ transmission lines, the Commission’s

25             approach rejected discounting habitable structures already in proximity to existing lines


         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 13                           BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1             for purposes of evaluating prudent avoidance, absent evidence that the additional line

 2             would not increase or enhance EMF exposure. Ms. Hubbard offers no such evidence.

 3                    Accordingly, the Commission should count all habitable structures within 500 feet

 4             of the route centerline equally, consistent with its treatment in Dockets No. 38597 and

 5             45622. Under that standard, Route 894’s 85 habitable structures compare favorably to

 6             the 108 on Routes 891 and 895, and to the 139 to 173 on Ms. Hubbard’s remaining

 7             recommended routes.



 8   Q         MS. HUBBARD ARGUES THAT THE 500-FOOT THRESHOLD FOR IDENTIFYING

9              HABITABLE STRUCTURES IS INADEQUATE FOR 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINES.

10             WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE?

11   A         Even if a larger buffer were appropriate, it would need to be applied to all 122 routes, and

12             there is nothing in the record to suggest that Route 894 would gain proportionally more

13             habitable structures under an expanded buffer than any of Ms. Hubbard’s recommended

14             alternatives.   This is a criticism of the measurement standard, not a criticism of

15             Route 894’s relative performance. The comparative analysis in this proceeding was

16             conducted using the same 500-foot threshold for every route, and the Commission has

17             not adopted a different threshold for 765-kV projects.



18                             IV. RESPONSE TO JASON A. HOWTON

19   Q         MR. HOWTON OPPOSES LINKS F20 AND F23 AND RECOMMENDS FIVE

20             ALTERNATIVE ROUTES.            IS THERE A FILED ROUTE THAT ADDRESSES HIS

21             CONCERNS?

22   A         Yes. Route 899 is a filed route that avoids both Link F20 and Link F23. Route 899 uses

23             Links F21, E9, and G71 to bypass the corridor Mr. Howton opposes, while maintaining the




         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 14                           BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1             same alignment as Route 894 in every other portion of the route. Route 899 has 85

 2             habitable structures within 500 feet and an estimated cost of approximately $1.683 billion.

 3                    I identified Route 899 in my Direct Testimony as a route that could be considered

 4             if specific issues arose with Route 894.         Route 899 addresses Mr. Howton’s stated

 5             objection to Links F20 and F23 without requiring the Commission to approve a route with

 6             significantly more habitable structures.



 7   Q         HOW DO MR. HOWTON’S RECOMMENDED ROUTES COMPARE TO ROUTES 894

 8             AND 899 ON HABITABLE STRUCTURES?

9    A         The following table summarizes the comparison:


                                                           Table 3

                                            Comparison of Route 894 to
                                        Mr. Howton's Recommended Routes

                                                   Habitable
                                        Route      Structures        Estimated Cost

                                         894              85         $1,680,919,000

                                         899              85         ~$1,683,000,000
                                         296              105        $1,684,563,000
                                         194              95         $1,714,648,000
                                         767              135        $1,666,190,000
                                         551              146        $1,667,032,000
                                         546              151        $1,664,992,000


10                    Every one of Mr. Howton’s recommended routes has more habitable structures

11             than Routes 894 and 899. Route 296, his primary recommendation, has 105 habitable

12             structures (20 more than Route 894). Route 194 has 95 (10 more) but costs approximately




         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 15                           BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1             $34 million more. Routes 767, 551, and 546 have 135, 146, and 151 habitable structures,

 2             respectively.

 3                     Mr. Howton highlights Routes 551 and 546 as having the lowest ESA habitat

 4             exposure in the docket at 61 feet each. Route 894 has 461 feet of ESA habitat exposure.

 5             On a 223-mile route (approximately 1,177,000 feet), the difference between 461 feet and

 6             61 feet of ESA habitat exposure is 400 feet, or approximately 0.08 miles. Routes 551 and

 7             546 put 61 and 66 additional residences, respectively, within 500 feet of a 765-kV line to

 8             reduce ESA habitat exposure by approximately 0.08 miles on a 223-mile route.



9    Q         MR. HOWTON ARGUES THAT TARIFF EXPOSURE RENDERS THE APPLICANTS’

10             COST ESTIMATES UNRELIABLE AS A BASIS FOR COMPARING ROUTES. WHAT

11             IS YOUR RESPONSE?

12   A         Tariffs are a multiplicative factor, not a differentiating factor between routes. A 50% tariff

13             on steel increases the steel cost on each route by 50%. Because every route uses the

14             same types of materials and structures (steel lattice towers, ACSR conductor, and

15             associated hardware), the relative percentage difference between routes is likely

16             preserved under tariff conditions. While material mixes vary somewhat based on terrain

17             and structure type (angle versus tangent towers, foundation requirements), routes of

18             similar length and design voltage use broadly similar quantities of the same materials. A

19             route that is 2% less expensive before tariffs likely remains approximately 2% less

20             expensive after tariffs.

21                     If anything, tariffs slightly widen the absolute dollar gap between less expensive

22             and more expensive routes, because longer routes with more material absorb a larger

23             total dollar increase than shorter routes with less material. Route 894, at 223.17 miles, is

24             shorter and less expensive than several of Mr. Howton’s recommended alternatives.

25             Under the tariff conditions Mr. Howton describes, Route 894 does not become less


         SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
         PUC Docket No. 59475
         Page 16                           BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
  1             competitive; it becomes slightly more competitive on an absolute dollar basis.

 2             Mr. Howton’s estimated tariff exposure of $87.5 to $135 million would apply to every route

 3             in this proceeding, not uniquely to Route 894.



 4                            V. RESPONSE TO JAMES E. SCOTT, III
